name: Beta-carotene supplements
short: In a trial in male smokers, beta-carotene raised lung cancer 18% and deaths 8%. Given with vitamin A to smokers and asbestos workers: 28% more lung cancers, 17% more deaths.
text: In a randomised trial in 29,133 male smokers aged 50 to 69 in Finland, beta-carotene (20 mg a day) for five to eight years was followed by an 18% higher incidence of lung cancer and 8% higher total mortality, mainly from more deaths from lung cancer and ischaemic heart disease; it had little or no effect on other cancers. The CARET trial tested 30 mg beta-carotene plus 25,000 IU retinyl palmitate (vitamin A) daily in heavy smokers and asbestos-exposed workers (18,314 men and women at high risk of lung cancer) and was stopped 21 months early, with 28% more lung cancers and 17% more deaths in the active group; in its pre-specified analysis, lung cancer incidence (relative risk 1.36) and lung cancer mortality (relative risk 1.59) were higher than with placebo. A meta-analysis of 9 randomised trials found no effect on all cancers combined, but significantly higher incidence of lung cancer (relative risk 1.16) and stomach cancer (relative risk 1.34) with 20 to 30 mg a day, and concluded that these increased risks applied to smokers and asbestos workers. A meta-analysis of 31 randomised trials (216,734 participants) found no overall effect on mortality (risk ratio 1.02) but higher lung cancer mortality (risk ratio 1.14) and lower HIV-related mortality (risk ratio 0.55), and its authors warned against overstating either benefit or harm. The Finnish trial found no evidence of an interaction between beta-carotene and vitamin E on lung cancer incidence; no interaction data with medicines were found in the cited sources.
